entities.summary:
Avitus, born Marcus Maecilius Flavius Eparchius Avitus around 395-400 CE in Clermont-Ferrand, Gaul, served a brief but illuminating 14-month tenure as Western Roman Emperor from 455 to 456 CE. His ascent to the purple, largely orchestrated by the powerful Visigothic king Theodoric II, underscores the profound shift in power dynamics within the collapsing Western Roman Empire, where Germanic federates increasingly dictated imperial succession and policy. A Gallic aristocrat and a prominent general, Avitus's rule epitomized the challenges faced by the empire as it grappled with internal fragmentation, economic decay, and external barbarian pressures.

Prior to his imperial elevation, Avitus distinguished himself as a skilled diplomat and military commander under the Magister Militum Aetius. He played a crucial role in securing the Visigothic alliance that led to the decisive victory against Attila's Huns at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451 CE. Following the Sack of Rome by the Vandals in 455 CE, Avitus, then Magister Militum per Gallias, was proclaimed emperor in Arles on July 9, 455, with the strong backing of Theodoric II. His reign was marked by attempts to restore Roman authority in Gaul and Hispania, including successful campaigns against the Suebi, but his reliance on Visigothic support and his perceived Gallic bias alienated the Roman Senate and the Italian populace, who viewed him as a foreign imposition.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Avitus's short reign powerfully illustrates the terminal decline of the Western Roman Empire, showcasing the irreversible shift of power from Rome to barbarian federates and generals. His deposition by Ricimer further cemented the latter's role as kingmaker, directly shaping the subsequent imperial successions.
